exercises.title: Mapping the Urban Forest · Question 1
exercises.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
exercises.passage:
Mapping the Urban Forest

An inventory of city trees can reveal more than the number of trunks beside a street. By recording species, approximate size, and condition, planners can identify neighborhoods where trees are vulnerable to the same disease or where young trees receive little care. A map turns scattered observations into a picture that can guide decisions.

Residents can help collect this information, but an attractive online map is not sufficient evidence of accuracy. Volunteers may mistake similar species or measure trees in different ways. Training guides and repeated observations can make records more consistent. An uncertain identification can be flagged for an experienced observer rather than silently accepted as correct.

Participation is also uneven. A neighborhood with an active volunteer group may appear to have more trees simply because its streets have been surveyed more thoroughly. Planners therefore need to distinguish an empty space on the map from an actual absence of trees. Inviting volunteers to less frequently visited streets can reduce this imbalance.

Citizen mapping is most useful when local knowledge and careful procedures reinforce each other. Its value lies in producing information that is both broad enough to describe a city and reliable enough to support action.

options.text: Community tree maps can support planning when their data are collected and interpreted carefully.
Counting tree trunks is more useful than recording their condition.
Online maps provide a complete replacement for professional tree inspections.
Tree surveys mainly help cities compare the popularity of volunteer groups.

exercises.explanation: The passage explains the planning value of tree maps, then discusses identification errors and uneven coverage that must be addressed.

exercises.title: The Work of a Museum Replica · Question 1
exercises.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea?
exercises.passage:
The Work of a Museum Replica

A replica in a museum is sometimes treated as a substitute that is necessarily inferior to an original object. This view overlooks the different jobs that the two can perform. An original may preserve evidence about an artist's materials or working methods, while a carefully documented copy can make the object's shape and construction easier to investigate.

Some originals cannot safely remain on permanent display. Light, changes in humidity, or repeated handling may gradually damage them. A replica can permit close inspection or touch while the original rests in controlled storage. In this situation, the copy expands access without requiring the museum to expose the fragile object to additional risk.

Copies also have limitations. A smooth modern surface may conceal irregularities in the original, and a different material may change the apparent weight or color. For this reason, labels should explain what was reproduced and what was altered. Without that information, visitors could draw conclusions from features created by the copying process.

The important distinction is therefore not simply between authentic and inauthentic objects. It is between evidence that a particular object can provide and questions it cannot answer. A replica becomes an effective teaching tool when its purpose and limitations remain visible.

options.text: Replicas are most valuable when visitors cannot distinguish them from originals.
Original objects should generally be kept out of public exhibitions.
Modern copying methods reproduce every important feature of an object.
Replicas can expand learning and access when museums explain their purposes and limitations.

exercises.explanation: The author presents useful roles for replicas while emphasizing clear information about differences from originals.

exercises.title: A Library of Living Seeds · Question 1
exercises.prompt: What is the main purpose of the passage?
exercises.passage:
A Library of Living Seeds

Seed libraries apply the familiar idea of borrowing to a resource that can grow. Participants take seeds to plant and may later return seeds collected from their harvest. Unlike a book, however, a returned seed is not the same physical item that left the library. The collection is renewed through biological reproduction rather than the return of identical objects.

This difference creates useful possibilities. Gardeners can share plants that perform well under local conditions, and varieties overlooked by large commercial suppliers can remain available. The library also becomes a place to exchange practical knowledge about planting dates and care.

Yet maintaining a reliable collection requires more than accepting any packet that arrives. Seeds can lose viability during poor storage, and plants may cross with nearby varieties. A familiar name on a packet does not guarantee that the next generation will have all the expected characteristics. Recording where seeds came from and how they were grown helps participants understand these uncertainties.

A successful seed library therefore combines openness with documentation. New contributions make the collection diverse, while clear records allow gardeners to make informed choices. Its goal is not to promise perfect uniformity but to preserve a shared resource whose value depends on continued participation.

options.text: To show why borrowing is unsuitable for community gardening
To explain the opportunities and record-keeping challenges of seed libraries
To describe a method that prevents all changes in plant varieties
To compare the prices charged by seed libraries and commercial suppliers

exercises.explanation: The passage explains seed sharing and its benefits, then discusses storage, crossing, and documentation.

exercises.title: Listening to a City · Question 1
exercises.prompt: What is the central argument of the passage?
exercises.passage:
Listening to a City

Cities often describe noise using a single sound level. Such measurements are useful, but they cannot fully explain how a place is experienced. Two locations with similar readings may feel different if one contains passing traffic and the other contains a fountain or familiar conversation. The character and timing of a sound can matter as much as its intensity.

Sound maps attempt to preserve this richer picture. Researchers or residents record what they hear at particular places and times, sometimes adding short descriptions of the surrounding activity. Repeated visits can reveal how the same square changes from a quiet morning meeting place into a crowded evening route.

Interpreting these maps still requires caution. A short recording made during an unusual delivery may not represent an entire day. Participants also differ in what they notice and find disturbing. Combining recordings with measurements and accounts from several listeners gives a more nuanced description than relying on one source alone.

For planners, the aim need not be a city stripped of all sound. It can be to protect spaces where important activities remain possible: conversation near a bench, concentration inside a classroom, or rest beside a residential street. Sound maps help identify which changes might support those activities.

options.text: The main goal of city planning should be the elimination of public sounds.
Understanding urban sound requires context as well as measurements of loudness.
Sound recordings are reliable only when made in crowded city squares.
Residents generally experience sounds in the same way as researchers.

exercises.explanation: The author emphasizes character, timing, activities, and multiple sources of evidence alongside sound levels.

exercises.title: The Value of a Temporary Pool · Question 1
exercises.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
exercises.passage:
The Value of a Temporary Pool

A shallow pool that disappears during part of the year may look less valuable than a permanent pond. Its temporary nature, however, can create distinctive ecological conditions. Some organisms use the period when water is present to reproduce or develop, while the later dry period changes which other animals can remain there.

Seasonal pools cannot be understood only by looking at their wettest moment. Rainfall, shade, surrounding soils, and nearby vegetation affect how long they retain water. A pool that dries earlier in one year is not necessarily damaged; variation can be part of its normal pattern. Observations across seasons are therefore more informative than a single visit.

These habitats also depend on the land around them. Animals may use the water for one stage of life and nearby terrestrial habitat for another. Protecting only the visible basin can leave those connections vulnerable to roads or other changes outside its edge.

Recognizing the value of temporary pools calls for a broader definition of habitat. A place need not remain wet or look active throughout the year to support important biological processes. Its contribution may depend precisely on the alternation between conditions that a casual observer would consider complete opposites.

options.text: Permanent ponds provide a suitable replacement for every seasonal pool.
Temporary pools can be valuable habitats because of their seasonal changes and connections to surrounding land.
A pool that dries early should be restored to its maximum depth immediately.
The ecological value of water depends mainly on the visible size of its basin.

exercises.explanation: The author explains the roles of seasonal variation and land-water connections in these habitats.

The Value of a Temporary Pool

A shallow pool that disappears during part of the year may look less valuable than a permanent pond. Its temporary nature, however, can create distinctive ecological conditions. Some organisms use the period when water is present to reproduce or develop, while the later dry period changes which other animals can remain there.

Seasonal pools cannot be understood only by looking at their wettest moment. Rainfall, shade, surrounding soils, and nearby vegetation affect how long they retain water. A pool that dries earlier in one year is not necessarily damaged; variation can be part of its normal pattern. Observations across seasons are therefore more informative than a single visit.

These habitats also depend on the land around them. Animals may use the water for one stage of life and nearby terrestrial habitat for another. Protecting only the visible basin can leave those connections vulnerable to roads or other changes outside its edge.

Recognizing the value of temporary pools calls for a broader definition of habitat. A place need not remain wet or look active throughout the year to support important biological processes. Its contribution may depend precisely on the alternation between conditions that a casual observer would consider complete opposites.

exercises.title: Remembering an Event Together · Question 1
exercises.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
exercises.passage:
Remembering an Event Together

Oral histories preserve accounts that may never appear in official documents. A factory worker might describe how a machine sounded before it failed, or a resident might remember how neighbors organized during a flood. Such details can illuminate daily experience that formal records summarize only briefly.

Interviewers must nevertheless distinguish memory from a recording made at the time of an event. People interpret earlier experiences through what they learned later. Repeatedly hearing a shared story can also shape how an individual recalls the original occasion. These influences do not make an interview worthless; they change the kinds of questions it can help answer.

A careful oral-history project records the circumstances of the interview and preserves the speaker's own words. Researchers may compare different accounts with photographs, schedules, or other documents. When accounts diverge, the disagreement can itself reveal differences in position, responsibility, or later interpretation.

The goal is not always to force every speaker into a single consistent narrative. It is to understand both what people experienced and how they have made sense of it. Used in this way, oral history adds another dimension to the evidence rather than simply replacing written sources.

exercises.title: Designing for the Second Repair · Question 1
exercises.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
exercises.passage:
Designing for the Second Repair

The usefulness of a product depends partly on what happens after its first component fails. A device can have a durable outer case and still become unusable when a small internal part cannot be replaced. Repairable design considers this later stage instead of treating the sale as the end of the design process.

One approach is modular construction, in which major parts can be separated without destroying the rest of the product. Accessible fasteners and clear instructions can make that separation easier. Yet a removable part offers little benefit if compatible replacements disappear soon after the product reaches customers.

Repairability therefore involves a system of support as well as physical design. Replacement parts, diagnostic information, and people who can carry out repairs must remain available. A company might also need to document changes between product versions so that a part that looks identical is not installed in the wrong device.

There can be trade-offs. Making a case easier to open may complicate efforts to keep water out, and maintaining parts inventories requires resources. These challenges do not make repairable products impractical. They show why repairability should be planned from the beginning rather than added as a superficial feature at the end.

exercises.explanation: The passage discusses component access, continued support, documentation, and trade-offs.

exercises.title: What a Diagram Leaves Out · Question 1
exercises.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
exercises.passage:
What a Diagram Leaves Out

A diagram can make a complicated process easier to understand by leaving things out. A map of a transport network may show the order of stations clearly even when the lines do not follow the exact bends of streets. Its usefulness comes from selecting relationships relevant to a particular task.

This selectivity can also cause confusion. A reader who uses the same map to estimate walking distances may assume that equally spaced stations are equally far apart. The diagram has not necessarily been drawn poorly; it has been used to answer a question for which it was not designed.

Good explanatory diagrams make their priorities apparent. Labels, legends, and brief notes can indicate whether size, position, or sequence has been simplified. In teaching, comparing two representations of the same system can help learners notice these choices. One diagram may emphasize physical arrangement, while another emphasizes the flow of information.

The lesson is not that diagrams should contain every available detail. Excess detail can obscure the very relationship a learner needs to see. Instead, both makers and readers should ask what has been preserved, what has been omitted, and whether those decisions suit the intended purpose.

Transport diagrams should reproduce the exact shape of every street.
A diagram is useful when its simplifications fit the question the reader needs to answer.

exercises.explanation: The passage argues that selective representation is helpful but must match a task.

exercises.title: Navigation as Continuing Observation · Question 1
exercises.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea?
exercises.passage:
Navigation as Continuing Observation

Navigation is often imagined as following a fixed line from a starting point to a destination. In practice, many journeys also depend on continually observing the surroundings. A traveler may compare a remembered sequence of landmarks with the terrain ahead and revise a decision when conditions differ from expectations.

This kind of knowledge is more than a list of locations. Experienced travelers learn which features remain dependable and which change with weather, season, or human activity. A broad ridge may be a more persistent reference than a temporary path. Local knowledge can therefore include warnings about when a familiar clue should not be trusted.

Passing such knowledge to another person requires more than naming the landmarks. Descriptions must help the learner recognize them from a particular direction and understand their relation to other features. Accompanied journeys allow a learner to compare spoken explanations with what is actually visible.

Maps and instruments can complement this process by providing information that is difficult to judge directly. They do not remove the need to notice whether the real surroundings match the expected route. Navigation becomes a continuing exchange between prior knowledge, new observations, and decisions about what to do next.

Maps and instruments are useful only when local knowledge is unavailable.

exercises.explanation: The author presents navigation as an ongoing process of observation, comparison, and adjustment.

Navigation becomes a continuing exchange between prior knowledge, new observations, and decisions about what to do next.

exercises.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
exercises.passage:
When a Book Has Several Subjects

A library catalogue must help people find an item even when they approach it with different questions. A book about farming in a river valley might interest readers studying agriculture, environmental change, or the history of a particular region. Placing the physical book on one shelf does not settle how it should be described in the catalogue.

Classification systems offer consistency by using shared categories and naming rules. A reader who learns the system can transfer that knowledge to other searches. Yet categories reflect decisions about which differences deserve emphasis. A topic that is central to one community may be treated as a minor subdivision in a system developed elsewhere.

Effective description balances consistency, local relevance, and precision. The objective is not simply to attach more labels, but to create useful routes between a reader's question and a resource that can help answer it.

exercises.title: Small Finds and Everyday Meals · Question 1
exercises.prompt: What is the main point of the passage?
exercises.passage:
Small Finds and Everyday Meals

An archaeological site does not preserve every part of the life once lived there. Food and other organic materials may disappear while stone or pottery remains. This uneven survival can make everyday activities less visible than the durable objects associated with them.

Researchers therefore consider relationships among different kinds of evidence. Fragments of cooking vessels, animal bones, and plant remains can help them investigate how food was prepared or obtained. The location of a find is important: material recovered from a cooking area may have a different significance from a similar object found in a later deposit of mixed waste.

Interpretation also requires restraint. A few surviving remains cannot automatically establish the complete diet of an entire community. Preservation conditions and excavation choices affect what researchers recover. Comparing evidence from several areas can reveal patterns while also showing where the available record remains incomplete.

Ordinary fragments are valuable not because each supplies a complete story, but because they can contribute to a network of evidence. Their meaning depends on careful recording and comparison. An impressive object removed without information about its surroundings may answer fewer questions than a modest fragment whose context has been preserved.

Everyday archaeological finds become informative through context and comparison with other evidence.

exercises.title: Experiments Beyond the Laboratory · Question 1
exercises.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
exercises.passage:
Experiments Beyond the Laboratory

Field experiments allow researchers to study a process in the setting where it normally occurs. For example, an investigator interested in how people use a public space might compare seating arrangements in an actual courtyard. This can reveal practical behavior that a laboratory task might not reproduce.

The same realism creates difficulties. Changes in weather, nearby construction, or the timing of an event may affect the courtyard's use independently of the seating arrangement. If all the new seats are tested only on sunny afternoons, greater use cannot confidently be attributed to their design alone.

Researchers can respond by recording relevant conditions and planning comparisons carefully. Alternating arrangements across different days or comparing similar spaces can help separate a proposed explanation from competing ones. No arrangement removes every uncertainty, so reports should describe both the procedure and its limitations.

The strength of a field experiment is therefore not the absence of uncontrolled circumstances. It is the effort to identify and account for them while retaining a connection to everyday behavior. A result becomes more persuasive when readers can see why alternative explanations were considered and how the evidence bears on them.

Restoring the Connections of a Stream

An urban stream can look improved after its banks are planted and its channel is cleared. These visible changes may be valuable, but the stream receives water and materials from a much larger area. A narrow restoration site cannot be understood independently of the streets, drains, and land upstream.

For example, rainwater moving quickly across paved surfaces may enter a channel in sudden pulses. Changing only the vegetation beside one reach does not necessarily change that pattern. Restoring slower routes for water through soil or planted areas can address a process that begins outside the stream itself.

Restoration also involves connections along the channel. An obstacle may prevent organisms from moving between otherwise suitable areas. A successful project must therefore ask not only whether a location provides habitat, but whether the organisms that need it can reach it.

These broader questions complicate evaluation. A photograph can document greener banks, while observations over time are needed to understand changes in water movement or habitat use. The purpose of restoration is not merely to create a pleasing scene. It is to improve relationships among water, land, and living things that extend beyond the boundaries of a single construction project.

Designing with Moving Air

Natural ventilation uses the movement of air through openings to help maintain indoor conditions. In some buildings, windows on different sides allow air to pass through occupied rooms. In others, openings at different heights can support the movement of warmer air upward and outward.

The presence of openable windows does not by itself guarantee comfortable conditions. Outdoor temperature, wind, noise, and air quality all affect whether an opening can be used effectively. A design that works well during one season may require a different approach during another.

People's behavior matters too. An opening that is difficult to reach may remain closed, even when a designer expects it to be adjusted regularly. Clear controls and a building layout that occupants understand can therefore be as important as a theoretical description of air movement. Why Markets Need Organization

A marketplace may look like a spontaneous gathering of buyers and sellers, but regular exchange depends on coordination. People need to know where and when trading occurs and what arrangements govern access to the space. Even a temporary outdoor market relies on expectations shared by many participants.

Some rules solve practical problems. Clear routes between stalls allow visitors and deliveries to move through a crowded area. Agreed standards for displaying prices or measuring goods can reduce misunderstandings. Moving stalls to create a wider route can improve circulation but reduce the space available to individual vendors. Decisions about organization therefore distribute opportunities as well as solve logistical problems.

Understanding a market requires looking beyond the goods on display. Its physical layout and operating rules shape who can participate and how people interact. The appearance of informal activity may conceal an elaborate framework that allows the activity to continue.

exercises.title: Words That Travel · Question 1
exercises.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
exercises.passage:
Words That Travel

When a language borrows a word, it does not simply preserve a piece of another language unchanged. Speakers may adapt the word's pronunciation, spelling, or grammatical behavior to patterns they already use. Over time, a borrowed term can become so familiar that many speakers no longer think of it as foreign.

Meaning can change as well. A word used broadly in its source language may be adopted for a particular object or activity in the receiving language. Later speakers may extend it to new situations. The history of a word is therefore not always a reliable guide to every meaning it has acquired.

Dictionaries document these developments by examining evidence of actual use. A borrowed term may appear in specialist writing before spreading into ordinary conversation, or it may remain restricted to a small community. Editors need to distinguish a passing novelty from a usage that readers are likely to encounter repeatedly.

Borrowing illustrates how linguistic change depends on use rather than origin alone. A word's earlier form can help explain its route into a language, but the choices of later speakers shape what it becomes. Studying that process reveals contact between communities as well as change within a language.

options.text: Dictionaries prevent specialist vocabulary from entering ordinary conversation.
The origin of a word determines every meaning that later speakers give it.
Borrowed words can be reshaped by the speakers and uses of the receiving language.
Borrowed terms retain the pronunciation and meaning of their source languages.

exercises.passage:
Keeping Digital Records Usable

Preserving a digital record involves more than keeping a device in a safe cupboard. A file may remain physically stored while the hardware or software needed to open it becomes unavailable. Long-term access therefore depends on continued attention to the relationship between stored information and the tools used to interpret it.

Making copies in separate locations helps protect against loss, but copying alone does not ensure that the copies remain accurate or usable. Archives can check files for unintended changes and maintain information about how they were created. That documentation may explain a file's structure, its relationship to other records, or the conditions under which it was collected.

Sometimes a record is moved into another format to keep it accessible. This migration can preserve important content while changing features such as layout or interactive behavior. An archive must decide which characteristics matter for its purpose and document any transformations rather than assuming that every converted version is equivalent.

Digital preservation is thus an ongoing process rather than a single act of storage. The goal is not merely to keep something that can be called a copy, but to retain evidence that future users can locate, open, and interpret with an understanding of what has changed.

exercises.passage:
A Darker Route for Migrating Birds

Artificial light can change the conditions experienced by birds migrating at night. Brightly illuminated buildings may attract or disorient birds, drawing them away from their intended movement. Birds that circle a lighted area can expend energy and face a greater risk of colliding with nearby structures.

Reducing unnecessary nighttime lighting addresses one part of this problem. A building may need light for people using an entrance, while upper-floor decorative lighting serves a different purpose. Separating these needs allows managers to consider changes without assuming that every light must remain on throughout the night.

Timing is also important. Migration varies with season and conditions, so the same lighting practice may have different consequences at different times. Coordinated action by neighboring buildings can reduce a broader area of illumination than a change at one isolated property.

Darkening a building does not remove every hazard birds encounter during migration. Its value is more specific: it reduces an avoidable influence on nighttime movement. The example shows how conservation can involve reconsidering an ordinary human routine rather than creating a new habitat or handling individual animals directly.

exercises.prompt: Why does the author contrast entrance lighting with decorative lighting?
exercises.passage:
A Darker Route for Migrating Birds

Artificial light can change the conditions experienced by birds migrating at night. Brightly illuminated buildings may attract or disorient birds, drawing them away from their intended movement. Birds that circle a lighted area can expend energy and face a greater risk of colliding with nearby structures.

Reducing unnecessary nighttime lighting addresses one part of this problem. A building may need light for people using an entrance, while upper-floor decorative lighting serves a different purpose. Separating these needs allows managers to consider changes without assuming that every light must remain on throughout the night.

Timing is also important. Migration varies with season and conditions, so the same lighting practice may have different consequences at different times. Coordinated action by neighboring buildings can reduce a broader area of illumination than a change at one isolated property.

Darkening a building does not remove every hazard birds encounter during migration. Its value is more specific: it reduces an avoidable influence on nighttime movement. The example shows how conservation can involve reconsidering an ordinary human routine rather than creating a new habitat or handling individual animals directly.
